summary: A 1974 report on experiments with host output buffers on the Multics system to improve file transfer speed over the ARPANET. It is a practical note about tuning, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 662 reports a Multics experiment that used larger output buffers for file transfers. In the test, the new system transferred a file about four times faster than the old one.

questions: how did multics improve arpanet file transfer speed
subtitle: An experiment using larger Multics output buffers to improve file transfers.

tldr.problem: Multics used small IMP DIM output buffers and followed a one-message-at-a-time rule, which added overhead and limited file-transfer bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: The experiment added small buffers for interactive traffic and large buffers capable of holding the largest network message for bulk transfers.
tldr.outcome: For the tested file, average transfer rate rose from 6,837 to 27,578 bits per second; multiple transfers shared about 40,000 bits per second in total.

today: RFC 662 is a report of a Multics IMP DIM buffer experiment and its measured file-transfer rates.

sections.title: Why Multics File Transfers Were Slow
sections.content:
The RFC describes a need to transfer large amounts of data between Multics systems, including Multics System Tapes. A typical tape of approximately 12 million bits took about half an hour at then-current transfer rates.

The IMP Device Interface Manager (IMP DIM) used output buffers holding up to 940 bits. With a 72-bit header, the resulting message was at most 1,012 bits, so Multics sent single-packet messages even though the network could accept messages up to 8,096 bits. The system also followed an older protocol rule requiring it to wait for an RFNM before sending the next message on a connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Multics sent file data in small messages and waited for an acknowledgment before sending the next one. The author identifies both the small buffers and this wait as limits on transfer bandwidth.

sections.title: Small and Large Output Buffers
sections.content:
The revised IMP DIM used two buffer sizes. It selected a small buffer for a low amount of data, as with interactive users, and a large buffer for a larger amount such as a file transfer. The large buffer could hold the largest message allowed by the network.

Larger messages meant fewer messages and RFNMs for the same amount of data, reducing time spent in channel-driver programs and reducing idle time in the channel.
sections.plainLanguage: The revised system chose a small buffer for small interactive messages and a large one for file transfers. Fewer, larger messages meant fewer acknowledgments and less channel overhead.

sections.title: Transfer Measurements
sections.content:
The experiment compared transfers of the same file, approximately 2.5 million bits, using 36-bit bytes and Image mode. The service-to-development transfer using the old system averaged 6,837 bits per second; the development-to-service transfer using the new system averaged 27,578 bits per second.

The report estimates that a Multics System Tape of approximately 12.5 million bits would take about 7 minutes and 30 seconds at 27,500 bits per second. With two simultaneous transfers, total rate was about 40,000 bits per second, about 20,000 per transfer; with three, total remained about 40,000 bits per second, about 13,500 per transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: The file-transfer test was much faster with the new buffers. When several transfers ran at once, the total measured rate was about 40,000 bits per second and was shared among them.
